steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on learning to control a DC motor (golf cart steering) in real time with reinforcement learning. Cover the micromobility motivation, why real-time RL on physical systems is hard, why classical controllers fall short, our NFQ-based approach and simulator, and the headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Autonomous micromobility and DC motors; our focus
- RL successes vs need for offline simulation; difficulties with physical systems
- Our setting: real-time RL on a DC motor steering a golf cart; non-linearities
- Traditional position controllers and their limits
- Model-free RL and NFQ
- Simulator and its purpose
- Results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Micromobility
  - progress on full-size autonomous vehicles; autonomous micromobility also rising (cite): golf carts, scooters, bikes (cite each)
  - DC motor key component for these micro-transport vehicles
  - this work: control of DC motors for steering via RL in real time

- RL and physical systems
  - RL successes over past decade: games, robotics, NLP, intelligent transportation systems (cite each)
  - most RL needs offline virtual environment to collect many experiences faster than real-time
  - pronounced with deep neural networks: insufficient data -> poor fit, poor generalization
  - physical systems: 1) continuous state space; 2) no precise mathematical model of dynamics; 3) internal uncertainties (noise, inertia, control oscillation) and external perturbations (friction, timing restraints); 4) because of 1)–3) sim-to-real policy transfer not guaranteed

- Our setting
  - original idea of RL: policy learned, tested, improved in real time on physical system
  - continuous, non-linear dynamics; no knowledge of internal factors or external perturbations
  - position/angle control of DC motor attached to golf cart steering wheel: sequence of voltages to reach target position as fast as possible
  - non-linear because: temperature effect on resistance/impedance of motor coil, electromagnetic effects (cogging torque, eddy current), dead-zones (minimum voltage either polarity) from friction and variable load (cite)
  - hard to model these time-varying, interdependent factors together

- Traditional controllers
  - Bang-bang (cite), PID (cite), MPC (cite)
  - Bang-bang: max voltage one polarity until switching point, then opposite; oscillation, overshoot from inertia -> fails
  - PID: expert tuning, labor-intensive
  - MPC: anticipates future events, substitute for PID (no prediction); needs dynamic model, unavailable to us
  - supervised learning with neural nets for control (cite): static dataset, limited exploration, misses non-linearities/uncertainties of our system

- Model-free RL / NFQ
  - model-free RL (cite): data-driven, learns policy from reward feedback of interactions -> more promising
  - Neural fitted Q (NFQ) (cite): Q-value estimator improved iteratively from transitions on the physical system
  - NFQ used for cart-pole (cite), soccer playing robot (cite), real car (cite)
  - still: real-time DC motor position control without system knowledge or manual interference is challenging
  - our approach data-driven, applicable in any environment: DC motors in industrial, household, robotic processes

- Simulator
  - built from data collected on the physical system
  - purpose: 1) avoid hardware damage from acceleration and jerk under imperfect policy; 2) explore hyperparameters and learning strategies for NFQ (largely omitted in previous literature)
  - golf cart under sub-optimal policy amongst people could be dangerous
  - simulation transitions not the same as replaying stored memory: random initial position/state, may not match exactly due to approximation errors

- Results
  - no prior knowledge, only real-world interactions: policy learned in 10 minutes 35 seconds in hardware
  - some strategies/parameters for hardware chosen from simulator
  - simulator settings: network parameters =91, hint-to-goal size =2\%, linearly decaying exploration, network reset every 50 episodes, exponentially increased curriculum for position initialization
  - simulation: policy learned under one minute 53 seconds (average) on off-the-shelf laptop

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A lot of progress has been made in developing full-size autonomous vehicles, but autonomous micromobility, which includes golf carts, scooters and bikes, has also seen a rise. A key component that enables these micro-transport vehicles is the Direct Current (DC) motor. In this work we focus on controlling DC motors for steering with reinforcement learning (RL) in real time.

Over the past decade RL has had many successes in various applications such as games, robotics, natural language processing and intelligent transportation systems. But to learn an effective policy, most RL applications so far need an offline virtual environment where a large number of experiences can be collected much faster than real-time. This is even more the case when deep neural networks are combined with RL, because with insufficient data points a deep neural network will not fit properly and will not generalize well. If a physical system is involved, the learning task gets more complicated: 1) the system may have a continuous state space; 2) we may not have a precise mathematical model of the system dynamics; 3) the system will probably experience both internal uncertainties (noise, inertia, control oscillation) and external perturbations (friction, timing restraints); and 4) because of reasons 1)–3), it is not guaranteed that a policy transfers successfully from the virtual environment to the real world.

In this work we experiment with the original idea of RL, where an effective policy is learned, tested and improved in real-time on a physical system. The dynamics of the system are continuous and non-linear, and we assume no knowledge of the internal factors of the system or the perturbations from the external environment. Specifically, we consider position/angle control of a DC motor that is attached to the steering wheel of a golf cart: given a target steering position, we learn how to apply a sequence of voltages to reach that position as fast as possible. The system dynamics are non-linear because of many factors, including the influence of temperature on the resistance and impedance of the motor coil, electromagnetic effects (cogging torque, eddy current), and dead-zones (the minimum voltage required in either polarity to rotate the motor) caused by friction and variable load. These factors are time-varying and interdependent and it is difficult to model how they occur together mathematically, which makes the control task significantly more complicated.

Traditional approaches for position control of a DC motor go from a simple Bang-bang controller to more sophisticated methods like a Proportional Integral Derivative (PID) controller and a Model Predictive Controller (MPC). A Bang-bang controller reaches the desired position by applying a maximum voltage in one polarity until a switching point and then applying maximum voltage in the opposite polarity. But during this process the motor will oscillate and overshoot because of inertia, so it fails the task. A PID controller on the other hand needs an expert to tune the control parameters, which can be labor-intensive. MPC can anticipate future events before it exerts a control signal, and it has emerged as a substitute for the PID controller, which does not have predictive capabilities. But MPC needs a dynamic model of the system, and we do not have one. Recently supervised learning with neural networks has been proposed for control tasks, but these methods usually rely on a static dataset from limited explorations of the state space, so they do not cover the wide range of sources of non-linearities and uncertainties that are present in our physical system.

- Model-free RL / NFQ
  - model-free RL (cite): data-driven, learns policy from reward feedback of interactions -> more promising
  - Neural fitted Q (NFQ) (cite): Q-value estimator improved iteratively from transitions on the physical system
  - NFQ used for cart-pole (cite), soccer playing robot (cite), real car (cite)
  - still: real-time DC motor position control without system knowledge or manual interference is challenging
  - our approach data-driven, applicable in any environment: DC motors in industrial, household, robotic processes

- Simulator
  - built from data collected on the physical system
  - purpose: 1) avoid hardware damage from acceleration and jerk under imperfect policy; 2) explore hyperparameters and learning strategies for NFQ (largely omitted in previous literature)
  - golf cart under sub-optimal policy amongst people could be dangerous
  - simulation transitions not the same as replaying stored memory: random initial position/state, may not match exactly due to approximation errors

- Results
  - no prior knowledge, only real-world interactions: policy learned in 10 minutes 35 seconds in hardware
  - some strategies/parameters for hardware chosen from simulator
  - simulator settings: network parameters =91, hint-to-goal size =2\%, linearly decaying exploration, network reset every 50 episodes, exponentially increased curriculum for position initialization
  - simulation: policy learned under one minute 53 seconds (average) on off-the-shelf laptop

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A lot of progress has been made in developing full-size autonomous vehicles, but autonomous micromobility, which includes golf carts, scooters and bikes, has also seen a rise. A key component that enables these micro-transport vehicles is the Direct Current (DC) motor. In this work we focus on controlling DC motors for steering with reinforcement learning (RL) in real time.

Over the past decade RL has had many successes in various applications such as games, robotics, natural language processing and intelligent transportation systems. But to learn an effective policy, most RL applications so far need an offline virtual environment where a large number of experiences can be collected much faster than real-time. This is even more the case when deep neural networks are combined with RL, because with insufficient data points a deep neural network will not fit properly and will not generalize well. If a physical system is involved, the learning task gets more complicated: 1) the system may have a continuous state space; 2) we may not have a precise mathematical model of the system dynamics; 3) the system will probably experience both internal uncertainties (noise, inertia, control oscillation) and external perturbations (friction, timing restraints); and 4) because of reasons 1)–3), it is not guaranteed that a policy transfers successfully from the virtual environment to the real world.

In this work we experiment with the original idea of RL, where an effective policy is learned, tested and improved in real-time on a physical system. The dynamics of the system are continuous and non-linear, and we assume no knowledge of the internal factors of the system or the perturbations from the external environment. Specifically, we consider position/angle control of a DC motor that is attached to the steering wheel of a golf cart: given a target steering position, we learn how to apply a sequence of voltages to reach that position as fast as possible. The system dynamics are non-linear because of many factors, including the influence of temperature on the resistance and impedance of the motor coil, electromagnetic effects (cogging torque, eddy current), and dead-zones (the minimum voltage required in either polarity to rotate the motor) caused by friction and variable load. These factors are time-varying and interdependent and it is difficult to model how they occur together mathematically, which makes the control task significantly more complicated.

Traditional approaches for position control of a DC motor go from a simple Bang-bang controller to more sophisticated methods like a Proportional Integral Derivative (PID) controller and a Model Predictive Controller (MPC). A Bang-bang controller reaches the desired position by applying a maximum voltage in one polarity until a switching point and then applying maximum voltage in the opposite polarity. But during this process the motor will oscillate and overshoot because of inertia, so it fails the task. A PID controller on the other hand needs an expert to tune the control parameters, which can be labor-intensive. MPC can anticipate future events before it exerts a control signal, and it has emerged as a substitute for the PID controller, which does not have predictive capabilities. But MPC needs a dynamic model of the system, and we do not have one. Recently supervised learning with neural networks has been proposed for control tasks, but these methods usually rely on a static dataset from limited explorations of the state space, so they do not cover the wide range of sources of non-linearities and uncertainties that are present in our physical system.

Model-free RL is an alternative that is more promising for our task. It is a data-driven approach that tries to learn a control policy directly from the reward feedback of the controller's interactions with the system. One such algorithm is Neural fitted Q (NFQ), where a state-action Q-value estimator is improved iteratively using transitions that are collected from the physical system itself. NFQ has been used to learn control policies for a cart-pole system, a soccer playing robot and a real car. But learning to control the position of a DC motor automatically in real-time, without system knowledge or manual interference, is a challenging control task by itself. In this work the approach for learning a control strategy is data-driven and it can be applied to learn a control policy in any environment, i.e., under the specific uncertainties and non-linearities of the many applications of DC motors in industrial, household and robotic processes.

Besides the real-world experiments, we also build a simulator with the data collected from the physical system. The simulations have two purposes: 1) to prevent damage to the hardware from the acceleration and jerk caused by an imperfect policy; and 2) to experiment with a wide range of hyperparameters and learning strategies for NFQ, which is a study that previous literature has mostly left out. Also, operating a golf cart in the real world under a sub-optimal policy and amongst people could be physically dangerous. The simulated environment is built from real-world data, but making transitions in the simulation is not the same as retrieving them from stored memory: every episode starts from a randomly initialized position (so also a randomly initialized state), which may not always have an exact match in simulation because of approximation errors.

As a result, starting without prior knowledge and only relying on real-world interactions, we successfully learned a control policy in hardware in 10 minutes and 35 seconds. Some of the strategies and parameters used for learning in hardware were determined from a simulator. Using the results of the simulator experiments (number of neural network parameters =91, hint-to-goal size =2\%, linearly decaying exploration strategy, neural network reset frequency = every 50 episodes, and exponentially increased curriculum learning for position initialization), we also successfully learned a control policy in simulation in under one minute and 53 seconds (on average) on an off-the-shelf laptop.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
While significant progress has been made in developing full-size autonomous vehicles, autonomous micromobility, including golf carts [1], scooters [2,3], and bikes [4,5], has also seen a rise [6]. A key component enabling these micro-transport vehicles is the Direct Current (DC) motor. In this work, we focus on the control of DC motors for steering via reinforcement learning (RL) in real time.

RL has seen many successes over the past decade in various applications such as games [7,8], robotics [9], natural language processing [10], and intelligent transportation systems [11,12]. However, to learn an effective policy, most RL applications to date require an offline virtual environment for collecting a large number of experiences much faster than real-time. This is pronounced when deep neural networks are combined with RL, since insufficient data points will not fit a deep neural network properly and let it generalize well. The learning task is further complicated if a physical system is involved: 1) the system may contain a continuous state space; 2) we may lack a precise mathematical model of the system dynamics; 3) the system is likely to experience both internal uncertainties (noise, inertia, control oscillation) and external perturbations (friction, timing restraints); and 4) due to reasons 1)–3), successful policy transfer from the virtual environment to the real world is not guaranteed.

In this work, we experiment with the original idea of RL, where an effective policy is learned, tested, and improved in real-time on a physical system. The system dynamics are continuous and non-linear, and no knowledge is assumed of the internal factors of the system or of external environment perturbations. Specifically, we consider position/angle control of a DC motor attached to a golf cart steering wheel: given a target steering position, we learn how to apply a sequence of voltages to reach that position as fast as possible. The system dynamics are non-linear due to many factors, including the influence of temperature on the resistance and impedance of the motor coil, electromagnetic effects (cogging torque, eddy current), and the presence of dead-zones (minimum voltage required in either polarity to rotate the motor) caused by friction and variable load [13,14]. The difficulty of mathematically modeling these time-varying and interdependent factors occurring together significantly complicates the control task.

Traditional approaches to position control of a DC motor range from a simple Bang-bang controller [15] to more sophisticated methods such as the Proportional Integral Derivative (PID) controller [16] and the Model Predictive Controller (MPC) [17]. To reach the desired position, a Bang-bang controller applies a maximum voltage in one polarity until a switching point, and then applies maximum voltage in the opposite polarity. However, during this process the motor will experience oscillation and overshoot errors due to inertia, and thus fails the task. A PID controller, on the other hand, requires an expert to tune the control parameters, which could be labor-intensive. MPC, which can anticipate future events before exerting a control signal, has emerged as a substitute for the PID controller (which lacks predictive capabilities). However, MPC requires a dynamic model of the system, which is not available to us. Recently, supervised learning with neural networks has been proposed for control tasks [18], but these methods usually rely on a static dataset from limited explorations of the state space, and hence do not cover the wide range of sources of non-linearities and uncertainties present in our physical system.

As an alternative, model-free RL [19], a data-driven approach that aims to learn a control policy directly from reward feedback on the controller's interactions with the system, is more promising for our task. One such algorithm is Neural fitted Q (NFQ) [20], in which a state-action Q-value estimator is iteratively improved using transitions collected from the physical system itself. NFQ has been used to learn control policies for a cart-pole system [20], a soccer playing robot [21], and a real car [22]. However, learning to automatically control the position of a DC motor in real-time without system knowledge or manual interference is a challenging control task in itself. In this work, the approach to learning a control strategy is data-driven and can be applied to learn a control policy in any environment, i.e., under the specific uncertainties and non-linearities of the numerous applications of DC motors in industrial, household, and robotic processes.

In addition to the real-world experiments, we build a simulator using the data collected from the physical system. The purpose of the simulations is to 1) prevent damage to the hardware from acceleration and jerk induced by an imperfect policy; and 2) experiment with a wide range of hyperparameters and learning strategies for NFQ, a study largely omitted from previous literature. Moreover, operating a golf cart in the real world under a sub-optimal policy and amongst people could be physically dangerous. Although the simulated environment is built from real-world data, transitions made in simulation are not equivalent to retrieving them from stored memory: every episode starts from a randomly initialized position (and hence a randomly initialized state), which may not always have an exact match in simulation due to approximation errors.

As a result, starting without prior knowledge and relying solely on real-world interactions, we successfully learned a control policy in hardware in 10 minutes and 35 seconds. Some of the strategies and parameters used for learning in hardware were determined from a simulator. In addition, using the results of the simulator experiments (number of neural network parameters =91, hint-to-goal size =2\%, linearly decaying exploration strategy, neural network reset frequency = every 50 episodes, and exponentially increased curriculum learning for position initialization), we also successfully learned a control policy in simulation in under one minute and 53 seconds (on average) using an off-the-shelf laptop.
